title: Seven weeks
hook: he stays near the tree; in a storm the serpent Mucalinda coils around him as shelter

segments.voice: Yesterday, the house-builder: craving, seen at last, its rafters broken. Your line was house-builder, you are seen. Which habit did you name? Day fifty-seven, and a new week: setting the wheel turning.

After something enormous happens, a birth, a death, a graduation, a diagnosis, most of us want to rush straight to the next thing. Tell everyone. Make plans. Post about it. And sometimes the wisest thing is the opposite. Stay. Let it settle. The Buddha has just woken up, under the tree, at dawn. You might expect him to leap up and head for the nearest town to share it. He doesn't. The tradition says he stays right there, near the tree, for seven weeks. And sometime in those weeks, a great storm rolls in. Today, seven weeks.
screen: `AFTER SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `STAY. LET IT SETTLE.` → `A GREAT STORM ROLLS IN.`

segments.voice: The later telling gives each week its own place. In the first, he sits on the same seat, taking in the freedom. In another, he stands and gazes at the tree without blinking, in gratitude. In another, he walks slowly up and down. And in one of those weeks, he sits beneath a tree called the Mucalinda tree. That's when the storm comes. It isn't a passing shower. For seven days, the sky is black and the rain doesn't stop. Cold winds blow. And from under the ground comes Mucalinda, the serpent king who lives there, a naga, a great snake-being of Indian tradition. Mucalinda coils his long body around the Buddha seven times and spreads his great hood over his head like an umbrella. Not to threaten him. To protect him. Keep off the cold, keep off the heat, keep off the flies and the wind. And when the storm passes, the serpent unwinds, takes the form of a young man, and bows. This scene is in the Udana, one of the older collections. And it became one of the most beloved images in Buddhist art, especially in Cambodia and Thailand: the Buddha seated on the coils of a great serpent, its many heads fanned out above him like a crown. What does it teach? The one who has woken up is not alone in the world. Even a creature many people fear comes to shelter him. After the struggle and the storm, the story lets him be held. Sheltered.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS NEAR THE TREE.` · `SEVEN DAYS OF STORM.` · `MUCALINDA COILS AND SPREADS HIS HOOD.` · `A SERPENT AS SHELTER.` · then, large: `SHELTERED.`

segments.voice: Find somewhere sheltered to sit, if you can: under a roof, near a wall, wrapped in a blanket. Notice the shelter around you. The walls that keep off the wind. The roof that keeps off the rain. The clothes on your skin. Let yourself feel held by them, the way the Buddha was held by the serpent's coils. You don't have to earn it right now. You're just sheltered. Breathe, and let the body soften inside that shelter. The bell holds the time.
Seven weeks. The time the Buddha stayed near the tree after waking, when, in one great storm, the serpent Mucalinda coiled around him as shelter.
Your line: sheltered. Today, when you're inside while it's cold, hot or wet outside, stop for one breath and notice what's holding you. Day fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Images of the Buddha seated on the coils of the naga Mucalinda are common in Cambodia and Thailand, where the image is also associated with a day of the week, and Buddhists retell the seven weeks as the time he dwelled in the freedom of awakening.

fork.setup: you're a great serpent living under a tree. a seven-day storm breaks over the awakened one sitting above you. what do you do?
options: coil around him and spread your hood over his head.
wait for the storm to pass, then visit.
fork.reveal: Mucalinda coils around him seven times and spreads his hood like an umbrella. when the storm passes, he takes human form and bows.

original.note: Pali: the name of the naga king, and of the tree he lived beneath.

trapdoor: what you thought: a snake wrapped itself around the Buddha.
what it means: a serpent king sheltered the awakened one through a seven-day storm. after the struggle, he's held.
what a scholar hears: Udana 2.1 (Mucalinda Sutta) and Vinaya Mahavagga 1.3; the seven-week sequence at named sites is fully laid out in the Nidanakatha.

sources.ref: Mucalinda Sutta (Udana 2.1): the naga shelters the Buddha
Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.1–1.4: the weeks after the awakening
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the seven weeks

notes: The Vinaya gives four sittings of seven days; the Nidanakatha expands to seven weeks at seven sites (the seat, the unblinking gaze, the jeweled walk, the jewel house, the Ajapala banyan, the Mucalinda tree, the Rajayatana tree). Confirm the week-by-week summary.
Mucalinda's shelter (seven coils, the hood; cold, heat, flies, wind) and his taking human form: Udana 2.1. Confirm.
The Mucalinda image as the Saturday Buddha in Thailand is mentioned only as 'associated with a day of the week' in howItsDone; confirm.
